newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan EVA to buy two Boeing 747s, two MD-11s.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan EVA to buy two Boeing 747s, two MD-11s.

text.p: Taiwan's EVA Airways, a unit of shipping giant Evergreen Marine, said on Monday it would buy two McDonnell Douglas MD-11 cargo planes and two Boeing 747-400 passenger planes in a deal worth US$600 million.
Contracts for the two Boeing jumbo jets were signed on Monday and those for the McDonnell Douglas planes would be signed in coming days, EVA said in a statement.
Delivery for the four planes would begin at the end of 1997 and bring EVA's fleet to 34 once complete, it said.
The four planes in effect will be bought from the same company if a proposed merger announced by Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp on Sunday is completed.
The longtime rivals said they expected to overcome any antitrust concerns under U.S. law.
EVA's new planes will be equipped with some of the 82 General Electric CF6-80 turbofan engines ordered from a GE unit in a US$750 million deal announced a week ago.
That deal triggered speculation that EVA was planning a purchase of as many as six Boeing or McDonnell Douglas jumbos, since the engines work on both makers planes.
"Because all the planes are equipped with GE engines, we will be able to strengthen the quality of our flight safety and save on maintenance and repair costs," EVA's statement said.
EVA said in May it was considering buying 10 or more Boeing 747-500 passenger planes, worth some US$200 million each.
EVA now flies 12 Boeing 747-400s for long-haul international routes, five Boeing 767-300s, four Boeing 767-200s, six McDonnell Douglas MD-11s and one newly delivered MD-90.
EVA took deliver in October of the first of six MD-90 planes bought from McDonnell Douglas in 1995.

The carrier, Taiwan's second international airline, made a net profit of T$198 million on sales of T$28.86 billion in 1995 after four years of losses since it began operations in 1991 and has ambitious growth plans.
Major new business could open if Nationalist-ruled Taiwan can find a way to end a five decade-old ban on direct flights between Taiwan and arch rival communist China across the Taiwan strait.
"We will continue to buy the most advanced planes to service our countrymen in accordance with the development of the market," the EVA statement said.
EVA has forecast three straight years of profits, including a targetted T$600 million on sales of T$35 billion in 1996, and plans to listed in the local stock market in 1998.
U.S. aircraft titans Boeing and McDonnell Douglas said in Washington on Sunday they would merge to create the world's largest aerospace company in a deal worth about $13.3 billion.
The combined firm, to be based at Boeing headquarters in Seattle and to operate under the Boeing Co name, was projected to have 1997 sales of about $48 billion, up from about $35 billion in 1996.
